worksheet.title: The Extra Block
worksheet.subtitle: Take out the block that goes too far
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a program by removing an extra block.

parts.title: Too far!
parts.text: Sometimes a program has one EXTRA block, so Bit goes too far and overshoots the target. Run the code, find the extra block, and cross it out to fix the program.

parts.title: Run it — too far
parts.prompt: Run Program 1 from 1. What number does Bit land on? It goes past the target 4.

parts.title: Remove the extra block
parts.prompt: Cross out ONE block so Bit lands exactly on 4. Which block did you remove? Run it again — what number now?

parts.title: You try — remove to fix
parts.prompt: Run Program 2 from 0. It lands on 0, not 1. Cross out ONE block so Bit lands on 1. Which block did you remove, and where does Bit land?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: If a program goes too far, it may have an extra block. Take out the one extra step so Bit lands right on the target.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students fix a bug where the program goes PAST the target because it has one extra block; they cross out the extra step and run again. Removing a step to fix the result is a kind of debugging. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: tape a number line 0 to 5 on the floor and mark the target, so students can walk the buggy program and feel Bit miss.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Run a program that overshoots the target — it has one step too many.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Program 1 lands on 5, past 4.
3. Let them try. Students cross out one block to land exactly on the target (Ex 2), then fix Program 2 (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Program 1: 1 → 3 → 4 → 5. Bit lands on 5, past the target 4.
Exercise 2 — remove one "forward 1": 1 → 3 → 4. Bit lands on 4.
Exercise 3 — Program 2: 0, forward 2 → 2, back 1 → 1, back 1 → 0. Remove one "back 1": 0 → 2 → 1. Bit lands on 1.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing a block instead of removing one. Here the fix is to take a step away.
Make it easier: walk the program and notice the step that goes one too far.
Make it harder: ask how many steps past the target Bit went, and why that points to one extra block.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students follow (or write) step-by-step instructions, in order, to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a program, change a block to fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child removes the one extra block so Bit lands exactly on the target.
